reference_action: Overgrown woody basil: remove old stalk, focus on smaller shoots and prune just above Y-shaped side shoots; OP confirms pruning plus moving outside caused vigorous growth.

sources.reason: Explicitly prune a quarter inch above paired leaf buds/side shoots and repeat for bushiness, directly matching the validated pruning. Old woody-stalk removal and outdoor relocation are not explicit.

Comments explain removing center stalks and pruning branches while leaving at least one node to regrow, matching the central pruning action. Linked image guide is not needed for this text-supported hit.
Short has a pruning title but no captured cutting instructions or transcript.
Only the first caption fragment and general pruning title are visible; propagation comment does not confirm where to cut for the validated bushier-growth remedy.
Short title is visible but the pruning method is unavailable.

actions.action: Select slow-bolting or sterile variety for future planting
Inspect nodes and cut stems a quarter inch above side shoots, removing about a third
Check and repeat pruning about every two weeks
Apply liquid organic fertilizer after large harvest
Provide sunshine draining soil and consistent moisture
Check weekly and remove flower buds
Shear flowers from small-leaved Greek basil as alternative

resolved.reason: Correctly addresses insufficient pruning and supplies the validated above-node cut for bushier growth, with no likely harmful instruction.

harmfulness.reason: Removing “about one-third” and leaving healthy leaf buds protects regrowth, and sharp pruners avoid tearing. Fertilizer after harvest lacks a dose and is an unnecessary extra, but the main pruning method is low risk.

specificity_accuracy.reason: “Cut the main stem about a quarter inch above the leaf buds” directly matches the reference Y-shaped side-shoot instruction. It does not specifically identify this plant’s old woody stalk or advise moving it outside.

feasibility.reason: Cut location, fraction removed and weekly/two-week checks are concrete and use fingers or ordinary snips. Optional plant separation and fertilizer add effort and some ambiguity beyond the otherwise simple pruning task.

generic_phrases: plenty of sunshine, well-drained soil, and consistent moisture

      - listitem: To stimulate growth. I know, I know, it doesn’t make a lot of sense to remove part of a plant to make it grow, but trust me, this is the best way to force your basil to grow big and bushy.       - text: To remove flowers. Eventually most basil plants produce flowers. The flowers are very attractive to bees but basil plants that are allowed to flower slow down their vegetative growth.       - text: is also very slow to flower. Or, you can plant a variety like Pesto Perpetuo which is sterile and doesn’t produce flowers at all.

- heading "When to trim basil" [level=2]
    - paragraph: Timing, as they say is everything. And when trimming basil it’s best to start early when the seedlings are about six to eight inches tall and have three to four sets of leaves. At that point, each plant is likely a single stem. I like to pinch that main stem back to a strong set of side shoots, removing about one-third of the plant. This simple trimming DOUBLES your basil harvest by turning single stemmed plants into double stemmed plants. How easy is that?

    - paragraph: In the above paragraphs I outlined how to trim back basil seedlings for the first time to stimulate growth. But what if you’re not growing your own seedlings? What if you bought basil transplants from the garden centre and they’re already bigger than six to eight inches tall? Don’t worry! You can still trim these back to thicken up the plants and encourage growth. Then, trim the plants back by about one-third, clipping just above a set of side shoots.

      - text: are ideal for cutting herbs back). I often use my fingers for pinching flowerbuds or trimming top shoots of basil, but if you’re cutting the plants back hard, you may need sharp pruners as you don’t want to tear the stems.     - paragraph: Before you start clipping or pinching, take a close look at the plant. You want to cut central stems back to a lower set of leaves where two tiny leaf buds emerge from the leaf axil. You can remove just a few stems to flavor your dinner or cut the plant back by a third to gather enough basil to make pesto or to preserve.

    - heading "How to pinch out basil flowers" [level=2]
    - paragraph: As noted above, another reason to learn how to trim basil is to remove flowers. Stressed out basil plants begin to flower sooner than those given plenty of sunshine, well-drained soil, and consistent moisture. Therefore, aim to keep your basil happy so that it keeps producing leaves, not flowers. But for most types of basil, it’s inevitable that you’ll see flower buds forming by mid summer.

      - img "summer herb garden maintenance"
      - generic: Removing basil flowers as they form re-directs energy into vegetative growth and can result in a bigger harvest.
    - heading "How to remove flowers on Genovese basil plants" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: It’s easy to spot flowerbuds on
      - link "Genovese basil":
        - /url: https://www.awin1.com/cread.php?awinmid=95143&awinaffid=2084321&ued=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.highmowingseeds.com%2Forganic-non-gmo-genovese-basil.html
      - text: plants. They emerge at the tip of the shoots and look like a dense cluster of tiny leaves. As they grow, the flowerbuds elongate and tiny white flowers emerge (or purple flowers on Thai basil). I like to pinch the buds as soon as I notice them forming. That way, the plant doesn’t expend unnecessary energy on those buds.
    - paragraph: You can use your fingers to trim off flowerbuds or you can use garden snips. Whatever you find most comfortable. After that initial flower pinching, you’ll need to check every week or so for new flowerbuds and remove those as they appear.
    - heading "Trimming basil flowers on Greek basil plants" [level=2]
    - paragraph: Greek basil plants form tight, tidy balls that grow up to a foot wide and tall. They have many small leaves with flowerbuds forming at the tips of each shoot. Hand pinching buds or flowers from these plants takes some time so I cheat a bit by using my mini herb snips or even garden shears. Just shear the flowers off like you would shape a boxwood hedge. The plants respond to this type of trimming by continuing to pump out more foliage.
